data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Naval strategy often uses probabilistic risk assessment which Popper rejects.","War outcomes are singular events, whereas scientific tests aim for universal laws.","Strategic selection may rely on intelligence (induction) about enemy habits."],"overturn_conditions":["If the war games (tests) are biased or irrelevant to actual combat conditions.","If the enemy (nature) changes strategies fundamentally between simulation and reality."],"shared_structure":["Selection of a plan based on surviving simulated attacks rather than proven success.","Preference driven by robustness against known failure modes, not probability of victory.","Action taken on the 'least refuted' option despite uncertainty of outcome."],"source_memory_refs":["naval_strategy_selection"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a commander chooses the plan that survived the most rigorous war games, a scientist chooses the theory that survived severe tests.","Robustness in simulation correlates with robustness in reality without guaranteeing success."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a rational methodological choice grounded in verisimilitude (truth-likeness) rather than inductive probability; accepting this costs the scientist any claim to certainty or justified belief in the theory's truth, restricting rationality to the critical selection of the best available conjecture for further testing.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined or compared without relying on inductive assumptions about future performance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for survival implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature (that what worked before will work again).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own later admissions regarding the undefinability of verisimilitude undermine the comparative basis for preference.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification of truth' (which requires induction and is rejected) and 'rationality of action' (which relies on comparative verisimilitude). A theory that survives severe tests has withstood attempts at falsification, suggesting it possesses higher content and closer approximation to truth (verisimilitude) than a falsified or untested rival. Therefore, preferring it is not an inductive leap that it *will* hold, but a critical judgment that it is currently the *best candidate* we have, making it the only rational basis for action and further inquiry without smuggling in probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
